subject: Mathematics
source: National Curriculum (KS2 Year 4: place value to 10,000, rounding, Roman numerals, negative numbers; addition and subtraction; times tables to 12 x 12)

lessons.title: Thousands, hundreds, tens and ones
objectives: Read and write 4-digit numbers in numerals and words
State the value of each digit in a number up to 9999

keywords.def: groups of one thousand; the left digit of a 4-digit number
the value a digit has from its position
one of the symbols 0 to 9

starter: Say Bismillah. Write four hundred and seven as a number.
What is the value of the 6 in 862?

teach.heading: Ten hundreds make a thousand
teach.note: Use place value counters or a place value chart with Th, H, T, O. Each place is ten times the one to its right. Ask what comes after ten thousands.

teach.heading: Reading 4,365
bullets: Four thousand, three hundred and sixty-five.
teach.note: Build the number with counters. Say it aloud. Common error: reading 4,365 as 'four three six five'.

teach.heading: Zero as a placeholder
bullets: 5,070 has no hundreds and no ones.
Each zero keeps a digit in position.
teach.note: Compare 5,070, 570 and 5,700 in a place value chart. Pupils often write five thousand and seventy as 5,0070.

teach.heading: Commas and spaces
teach.note: Mention that 4-digit numbers can be written 4365 or 4,365. 9,999 + 1 = 10,000 is a key idea.

practice: What is the value of the 3 in 6,342?
Write 'nine thousand and forty' as a number.
independent: Write as numbers: 3 thousands 5 hundreds 2 tens 1 one; 8 thousands 0 hundreds 4 tens 0 ones; five thousand six hundred.
State the value of the digit 7 in: 7,031; 5,672; 2,917; 9,007.
Write these in words: 4,018; 6,500; 8,999.
exit: What is the value of the 5 in 3,512?
Write 'two thousand and sixteen' as a number.
lessons.homework: Write six 4-digit numbers from things you see (for example a house number, a price) and write them in words.
lessons.send: SEND: place value chart with counters. EAL: pre-teach thousand/hundred vocabulary. Stretch: numbers to 100,000.

lessons.title: Partitioning and 1000 more or less
objectives: Partition 4-digit numbers in different ways
Find 1000, 100 and 10 more or less than a number

keywords.def: split a number into parts
add to or take from a number by a given amount

teach.heading: Standard partition
teach.note: Show a part-whole model with four parts. Ask pupils to say each part's value.

teach.heading: Flexible partition
teach.note: Exchange one thousand for ten hundreds. This is the basis of column subtraction.

teach.heading: 1000 more, 1000 less
teach.note: Crossing 10,000 and 1,000 are tricky: 1000 less than 1,200 is 200.

teach.heading: 100 and 10 more or less
teach.note: Take care with crossing boundaries. 4,005 - 10 = 3,995 as the thousands digit changes.

independent: Complete the table of 1000 more, 1000 less, 100 more, 100 less for 2,750; 6,008; 9,950.
lessons.homework: Choose five 4-digit numbers and find 1000, 100 and 10 more and less for each.
lessons.send: SEND: use place value counters on a chart. Stretch: use 5- and 6-digit numbers.

lessons.title: Comparing and ordering 4-digit numbers
objectives: Compare 4-digit numbers using <, > and =
Order numbers in ascending and descending order

keywords.def: in order from smallest to largest
in order from largest to smallest

teach.heading: Start from the left
teach.note: Always compare the highest place value first. Use a place value chart with numbers one above the other.

teach.heading: Number of digits
bullets: More digits means a larger number.
teach.note: Only valid when there are no leading zeros. Ask pupils why a number with more digits is larger.

teach.heading: Ordering lists
teach.note: Use a systematic approach: group by hundreds, then tens.

teach.heading: Missing digits
bullets: What digits could go in the box?
Digits 6, 7, 8 or 9... wait, check the tens place.
teach.note: Careful: in 6,4_2 the blank is the tens digit; for 6,4_2 > 6,452 the digit must be 6, 7, 8 or 9? No: compare 6,4?2 with 6,452: tens digit must be 5 or more with ones 2 vs 2 equal, so 6,452 equals itself at 5; > needs 6 to 9. Discuss and verify with pupils.

independent: Using digits 2, 4, 6 and 9 once each, make the largest and smallest 4-digit numbers.
lessons.homework: Write down ten 4-digit numbers using the digits 1, 3, 5 and 7, then order them.
lessons.send: SEND: use digit cards and a chart. Stretch: compare numbers up to 100,000.

lessons.title: Rounding to the nearest 10
objectives: Round numbers to the nearest 10
Understand the rule for numbers ending in 5

keywords.def: change a number to a nearby, simpler one
the closest multiple of ten

teach.heading: On a number line
teach.note: Mark 60, 65, 70 and place 63. Ask why 65 is a special point.

teach.heading: The rule
teach.note: 5 rounds up by convention (halfway rounds up). Make sure pupils know the rule and why.

teach.heading: Bigger numbers
teach.note: Show the tens carrying over: 3,995 rounds up to 4,000. This is a common misconception area.

teach.heading: Why round?
bullets: Estimates are easier to work with.
Say 'about 50' when exact is not needed.
teach.note: Link rounding to everyday contexts like prices and distances. Ask pupils where rounding is useful.

independent: Round to the nearest 10: 34; 75; 506; 2,148; 3,999.
A number rounds to 80. What could it be? List all whole numbers.
True or false: 4,455 rounds to 4,450.
lessons.homework: Round ten numbers you find at home (e.g. prices, distances) to the nearest 10.
lessons.send: SEND: use a number line with the halfway point marked. Stretch: rounding decimals to the nearest whole number.

lessons.title: Rounding to the nearest 100
objectives: Round numbers to the nearest 100
Decide using the tens digit

keywords.def: the closest multiple of one hundred
exactly in the middle between two numbers

teach.heading: Between hundreds
teach.note: Use the number line with 450 marked. Compare with rounding to 10.

teach.heading: The tens digit decides
bullets: 0 to 4: stay the same, ones go to zero.
teach.note: Show 463 -> tens digit 6 -> up to 500. And 438 -> tens digit 3 -> down to 400.

teach.heading: Bigger numbers
teach.note: Work through the carrying: 6,951 has tens digit 5 so round up to 7,000. Check by number line.

teach.heading: Error trap
bullets: Do not look at the ones digit.
Check the digit to the right.
teach.note: A common error is rounding 349 to 350 and then to 400. Rounding is done in one step, using only the digit to the right.

independent: A number rounds to 600. What is the smallest it could be? The largest?
Is 2,349 closer to 2,300 or 2,400? Explain.
lessons.homework: Collect five large numbers (e.g. populations, prices) and round each to the nearest 100.
lessons.send: SEND: scaffold with a number line and highlight the deciding digit. Stretch: rounding to the nearest 1000 and 10,000.

lessons.title: Rounding to the nearest 1000
objectives: Round numbers to the nearest 1000
Choose the correct degree of rounding

keywords.def: the closest multiple of one thousand
how exact a rounded number is, such as nearest 10 or 100

teach.heading: The hundreds digit decides
bullets: Hundreds digit is 6, so round up.
teach.note: Same rule, one place left. Halfway is 4,500; 4,628 is more than halfway.

teach.heading: Rounding down
teach.note: Emphasise replacing the lower digits with zeros. Show on a number line from 7,000 to 8,000.

teach.heading: Three levels
teach.note: Compare the three roundings for one number. Discuss which is most appropriate in different contexts.

teach.heading: In context
bullets: Rounding makes numbers easy to say.
teach.note: Use real contexts like numbers of pilgrims, book sales or distances. Never state invented statistics; use made-up values plainly.

independent: Round 4,768 to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000.
A number rounds to 3,000 to the nearest 1000. Write the smallest and largest whole numbers it could be.
lessons.homework: Write down five numbers and round each to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000.
lessons.send: SEND: use a three-row rounding grid. Stretch: round 5-digit numbers.

lessons.title: Roman numerals to 100
objectives: Read and write Roman numerals to 100
Convert between Roman and Hindu-Arabic numerals

keywords.def: a letter used for a number: I, V, X, L, C
the digits 0 to 9 we use today

teach.heading: The symbols
teach.note: Our usual digits came through the Arabic-speaking world from India, which is why they are called Hindu-Arabic numerals. Roman numerals were used in the Roman Empire.

teach.heading: Adding letters
teach.note: Larger values go first when adding. Never write more than three of the same letter in a row.

teach.heading: Subtracting
teach.note: A smaller value before a larger one is subtracted. Only I, X and C can be used to subtract. XIV = 14, XLIX = 49.

teach.heading: Converting
teach.note: Work from the largest. Ask pupils to say why 99 is XCIX and not IC.

independent: Write in Roman numerals: 8; 19; 44; 76; 99.
Write as numbers: XII; XXIV; LXXXIX; XCVIII.
Order from smallest: XIX, XL, XIV, LX, XC.
exit: What is XLIII as a number?
lessons.homework: Find three places that use Roman numerals (clocks, book chapters) and write them as numbers.
lessons.send: SEND: Roman numeral conversion chart. Stretch: Roman numerals to 1000 (D, M).

lessons.title: Negative numbers in context
objectives: Understand negative numbers using temperature
Order numbers including negatives

keywords.def: a number below zero
how hot or cold something is, in degrees Celsius
the number between positive and negative

teach.heading: Below zero
teach.note: Use a thermometer picture. Introduce the minus sign. Ask where negative numbers are used: temperatures, bank overdraft, floors below ground.

teach.heading: Number line
teach.note: Draw a line from -10 to 10. Point out that -2 is greater than -5 because it is further right.

teach.heading: Ordering
teach.note: Common error: thinking -7 is bigger than -2 because 7 is bigger than 2. Use temperature: -7 is colder.

teach.heading: Counting through zero
teach.note: Practise in steps of 1 and 2. Ask: how many steps from -3 to 2? (5)

independent: The temperature is 3 degrees. It falls by 5 degrees. What is the temperature now?
A lift goes from floor 2 down to floor -3. How many floors does it move?
exit: The temperature is -2 and rises by 5. What is it now?
lessons.homework: Look at a weather forecast for another country this week. Write down the temperatures and order them.
lessons.send: SEND: use a vertical thermometer model. Stretch: find differences between temperatures such as 8 and -5.

lessons.title: Place value review
objectives: Apply place value, rounding and negative numbers to problems
Reason with numbers up to 10,000

keywords.def: explaining why an answer is correct

teach.heading: Mixed problems
bullets: Choose the skill: place value, rounding, order.
teach.note: This lesson consolidates the unit. Work through each type with a worked example before pupils try.

teach.heading: Number riddles
bullets: My thousands digit is 3. I round to 3,500 to the nearest 100.
teach.note: Pupils find the full range. Ask for the smallest and largest.

teach.heading: Odd one out
teach.note: Encourage precise explanation. Several answers may be justified.

teach.heading: True or false
teach.note: XLV = 45, XXXIX = 39: true. -5 < -2: false. Ask pupils to prove each answer.

practice: Which numbers round to 5,000 to the nearest 1000?
Write the largest 4-digit number with digits adding to 10.
Is XC more or less than LXXX?
independent: A number rounds to 7,300 to the nearest 100. List five possible numbers.
The temperature in three towns is -4, 2 and -9 degrees. Order them and find the coldest.
Write 2,468 in two different partitioned ways, then round it to the nearest 10, 100 and 1000.
lessons.homework: Create a one-page place value fact sheet with an example for each skill.
lessons.send: SEND: choose fewer questions and use number lines. Stretch: write and solve your own riddle with five clues.

lessons.title: Column addition with 4-digit numbers
objectives: Add two 4-digit numbers using the column method
Add with exchanges in several columns

keywords.def: adding numbers written under each other, ones first
swap ten of one unit for one of the next unit

teach.heading: Set it out
bullets: Write Th, H, T, O above the columns.
teach.note: Use squared paper. Draw the headings to prevent misalignment. Pupils may need place value counters as support.

teach.heading: Worked example
teach.note: Show the carry digits under the line. Continue: hundreds 5 + 7 + 1 = 13: write 3, carry 1; thousands 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. Answer 6,343.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: It is close, so it is sensible.
teach.note: Always estimate. Ask: could the answer be 5,343? 16,343?

teach.heading: Different lengths
teach.note: Line up 328 under the last three digits. Pupils sometimes add 3 to the thousands column.

independent: Two schools have 1,456 and 2,378 pupils. How many altogether?
Find the missing digits: 3,_47 + 2,_36 = 6,083.
lessons.homework: Solve six 4-digit additions, estimating each first, and check with the inverse.
lessons.send: SEND: place value counters, grid paper. Stretch: add 5-digit numbers.

lessons.title: Column subtraction with 4-digit numbers
objectives: Subtract 4-digit numbers using the column method
Exchange across several columns

keywords.def: subtracting numbers written under each other, ones first
break one unit into ten of the unit below

teach.heading: Set it out
bullets: The larger number goes on top.
teach.note: Show the place value headings. Check that pupils place 6,432 above 2,185.

teach.heading: Exchange as needed
teach.note: Use counters. 6,432 becomes 6 Th, 3 H, 12 T... Step through: 2 ones need 10 from tens, so tens 3 become 2, ones 12; then tens 2 - 8 requires hundreds.

teach.heading: Finish
teach.note: After exchanging, the hundreds 3 become 2 and tens 2 become 12 (then 12 - 8 = 4); hundreds 2 - 1 = 1; thousands 6 - 2 = 4... Check this: 6,432 - 2,185 = 4,247, so the hundreds digit is 2: ones 12-5=7, tens 12-8=4, hundreds 3-1=2 (after giving to tens), thousands 4.

teach.heading: Check by adding
teach.note: Inverse check. Estimate too: 6,400 - 2,200 = 4,200.

independent: A stadium has 8,350 seats. 5,874 are sold. How many are left?
Spot the mistake: 5,204 - 1,865 = 4,461.
lessons.homework: Solve six 4-digit subtractions and check each with addition.
lessons.send: SEND: base ten and place value counters; a template with exchanges marked. Stretch: subtraction across zeros.

lessons.title: Estimating answers using rounding
objectives: Estimate sums and differences by rounding
Use estimates to check for errors

keywords.def: an approximate answer found by rounding
close to, but not exact

teach.heading: Round first
teach.note: Choose a sensible degree of rounding. Rounding to the nearest 100 gives 4,900 + 3,100 = 8,000. Nearest 1000 gives 5,000 + 3,000 = 8,000.

teach.heading: Estimating differences
teach.note: Compare with the exact answer 5,623. Ask which rounding gives the best estimate.

teach.heading: Is it reasonable?
teach.note: Use the estimate to check for large errors. Estimates do not prove the answer is exact.

teach.heading: Choose the rounding
teach.note: Discuss the trade-off. Ask when an estimate is enough, e.g. checking a shopping bill.

independent: Estimate by rounding to the nearest 100: 2,876 + 4,125; 8,432 - 3,589; 6,709 + 2,198.
Estimate by rounding to the nearest 1000 and compare to the nearest 100 estimate for 4,632 + 3,498.
Find the exact answers to the first three and say how close your estimates were.
lessons.homework: Estimate six calculations of your own choice, then calculate the exact answers.
lessons.send: SEND: use a rounding number line. Stretch: estimate with 5-digit numbers and decimals.

lessons.title: Two-step addition and subtraction problems
objectives: Solve two-step problems with 4-digit numbers
Use bar models to organise information

keywords.def: a diagram of bars showing how the amounts relate
needing two calculations to solve

teach.heading: Plan the steps
bullets: What do we need to find?
teach.note: Model reading aloud and annotating the question. A bar model clarifies parts and whole.

teach.heading: Worked example 1
bullets: A masjid collects 2,450 pounds in week 1 and 1,875 in week 2.
teach.note: Two steps: add, then subtract. Keep the context respectful and simple; this is just money in a fundraising example.

teach.heading: Check
bullets: Does the answer fit the story?
teach.note: Teach pupils to give the answer in context. Ask whether the answer should be bigger or smaller than the start.

practice: A train has 1,240 passengers. 485 get off and 362 get on. How many now?
A library has 7,500 books. It buys 1,260 and loans 2,845. How many on the shelves?
Which operation do we do first in each?
independent: A school raises 3,420 pounds in term 1 and 2,985 in term 2. They need 8,000. How much more?
A factory makes 5,620 toys in a week. 1,375 are sent to shop A and 2,480 to shop B. How many remain?
Write your own two-step problem with the answer 4,200.
exit: A shop has 4,500 mugs and sells 1,275 then 860. How many are left?
Draw a bar model for this problem.
lessons.homework: Write and solve three two-step word problems using 4-digit numbers.
lessons.send: SEND: use a template with step boxes. EAL: pre-teach vocabulary such as remain and altogether. Stretch: three-step problems.

lessons.title: Inverse operations and checking
objectives: Use the inverse operation to check calculations
Find missing numbers in additions and subtractions

keywords.def: an operation that undoes another
an unknown number in a calculation

starter: What is the inverse of adding 40?

teach.heading: Undoing
teach.note: Show on a number line. Use fact families with 4-digit numbers: 2,000, 1,500, 3,500.

teach.heading: Check by inverse
teach.note: Pupils use a subtraction to check an addition. Also 7,803 - 4,628 = 3,175.

teach.heading: Missing numbers
teach.note: Use a bar model with the unknown part. Then try 8,000 - __ = 5,125, found by 8,000 - 5,125.

teach.heading: Spot the error
bullets: That is not 5,000, so there is an error.
teach.note: Correct answer is 2,532. Ask pupils to find where the exchange went wrong.

independent: Check these using the inverse: 3,245 + 4,567 = 7,812; 9,000 - 3,456 = 5,544.
Write a fact family for 2,500, 3,750 and 6,250.
lessons.homework: Make a set of five missing number questions for a friend, with answers separately.
lessons.send: SEND: use a part-whole model. Stretch: missing digits in column calculations.

lessons.title: The 6 times table
objectives: Recall multiplication and division facts for the 6 times table
Use known facts to derive new ones

keywords.def: a number in a times table
the result of multiplying

teach.heading: Double the 3s
teach.note: Use the 3s you know. Show 6 x 7 as double 3 x 7 = 21 -> 42.

teach.heading: 5 and 1 more
teach.note: Show the array split. Decide which method pupils prefer.

teach.heading: The facts
teach.note: Chant and write. Note the pattern in the ones digits. Look for 6 x 6 = 36, 6 x 8 = 48.

teach.heading: Division
teach.note: Use the multiplication fact backwards. Ask for the fact family of 6, 8 and 48.

independent: Complete: 6 x 3, 6 x 9, 6 x 11, 6 x 12.
A pack has 6 eggs. How many in 7 packs? How many packs for 54 eggs?
lessons.homework: Practise the 6 times table for five minutes a day and test yourself.
lessons.send: SEND: use arrays and a times table square. Stretch: 6 x 14 using partitioning.

lessons.title: The 9 times table
objectives: Recall multiplication and division facts for the 9 times table
Spot patterns in the 9 times table

keywords.def: the sum of the digits of a number

teach.heading: Ten minus one
bullets: 9 x is 10 x less one group.
teach.note: Show the array: 10 rows minus 1 row. This method works for any 9 times fact.

teach.heading: The facts
bullets: Tens digit goes up, ones digit goes down.
teach.note: Pupils notice: for products up to 90 the digits add to 9. Ask why 108 breaks the pattern (1 + 0 + 8 = 9 still holds).

teach.heading: Finger trick
teach.note: A fun method. Use it for 9 x 1 to 9 x 10. Check against the pattern.

teach.heading: Division
teach.note: Use the facts backwards. Check by multiplying.

independent: Complete: 9 x 3, 9 x 7, 9 x 9, 9 x 11.
Nine children each have 9 marbles. How many altogether? Share 108 sweets among 9 children.
lessons.homework: Write out the 9 times table and colour the digit patterns you can see.
lessons.send: SEND: use the finger method and times table grid. Stretch: 9 x 15 as 10 x 15 - 15.

lessons.title: The 7 times table
objectives: Recall multiplication and division facts for the 7 times table
Use known facts to derive the remaining 7s

keywords.def: work out a new fact from one you already know

teach.heading: Facts you already know
teach.note: Most of the 7s are known from other tables by commutativity. Only 7 x 7 = 49 is new.

teach.heading: The new fact
teach.note: Use partitioning to derive. Ask pupils to find another route: 7 x 7 = 7 x 8 - 7 = 56 - 7 = 49.

teach.heading: All the facts
teach.note: Chant at speed. Practise recall with fast questions.

teach.heading: Division and problems
bullets: A week has 7 days: 9 weeks = 63 days.
teach.note: Use real context: days in weeks. 365 days is 52 weeks and 1 day (stretch).

independent: Complete: 7 x 4, 7 x 8, 7 x 11, 7 x 12.
A packet has 7 biscuits. How many in 9 packets? How many packets for 70 biscuits?
lessons.homework: Learn the 7 times table and test yourself with a timer.
lessons.send: SEND: highlight the 7s on a times table square. Stretch: 7 x 13.

lessons.title: The 11 and 12 times tables
objectives: Recall the 11 and 12 times tables
Use patterns to multiply by 11 and 12

keywords.def: something that repeats or follows a rule

teach.heading: The 11 times table
teach.note: Pupils notice the repeated digits. After 99 the pattern changes: 110, 121, 132.

teach.heading: 11 x 12
teach.note: Use partitioning for the harder facts. Show 11 x n = 10 x n + n.

teach.heading: The 12 times table
bullets: 12 x n = 10 x n + 2 x n.
teach.note: Partition 12 as 10 + 2. 12 x 7 = 70 + 14 = 84. A dozen is 12.

teach.heading: Division facts
teach.note: Use inverse. Ask how many months are in 12 years? (144)

independent: There are 12 months in a year. How many months in 9 years? A box holds 12 eggs; how many boxes for 96 eggs?
lessons.homework: Complete a full 12 x 12 multiplication grid from memory, then check it.
lessons.send: SEND: use a pre-filled grid and partitioning. Stretch: 11 x 25 and 12 x 15.

lessons.title: Multiplying three numbers; special numbers
objectives: Multiply three numbers together
Understand multiplying by 0 and by 1

keywords.def: a number that divides exactly into another
grouping numbers differently does not change the product

teach.heading: Multiply by 1 and 0
bullets: Any number x 1 stays the same.
teach.note: Use groups: 5 groups of 1 is 5; 5 groups of 0 is 0. Dividing by zero is not possible; avoid long discussion.

teach.heading: Three numbers
teach.note: We can group in any order. Look for easy pairs, such as 2 x 5 = 10.

teach.heading: Choose a clever order
teach.note: Pupils find the most efficient pairing. Check with the other order: 28 x 5 = 140.

teach.heading: Cuboid volumes
bullets: A box is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm.
teach.note: Link to volume as an application. Avoid formal volume work, just the idea of three numbers.

independent: Calculate: 2 x 6 x 5; 3 x 4 x 5; 2 x 9 x 5; 4 x 25 x 2.
Find the missing number: 3 x __ x 4 = 60.
Make 36 using three numbers multiplied together in two different ways.
lessons.homework: Write five three-number multiplication questions with a clever order for each.
lessons.send: SEND: use cubes to build boxes. Stretch: multiply four numbers together.

lessons.title: Factor pairs and times tables review
objectives: Find all the factor pairs of a number
Recall multiplication facts up to 12 x 12

keywords.def: two numbers that multiply to make a given number
a number that divides exactly into another

teach.heading: Factors
bullets: Factors divide exactly with no remainder.
teach.note: Link to the times tables: factors are the numbers in the table that multiply to make the target.

teach.heading: Factor pairs of 12
teach.note: List systematically: start with 1, then 2, then 3. Stop when the pairs repeat. The factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12.

teach.heading: Factor pairs of 36
teach.note: Square numbers have a factor pair with the same number. Count the factors of 36: 9, an odd number.

teach.heading: Review
teach.note: Short recall quiz, then problems. Pupils mark their own with the answers.

practice: Is 7 a factor of 42? Is 5 a factor of 42?
independent: Find all the factors of: 18; 28; 30; 45.
Find the number which has factor pairs 1 x 16, 2 x 8 and 4 x 4.
Complete a mixed times tables quiz of 20 questions.
lessons.homework: Find the factor pairs of ten numbers up to 50 and note any that have an odd number of factors.
lessons.send: SEND: use cubes to build arrays for each factor pair. Stretch: prime and composite numbers.
